body_markdown:
Here at ex-foundry/car commune/sh**box collective, we live and die by the magic of cross-referencing. It’s nearly impossible to keep everything running around the shop without an ever-growing database of junkyard parts that might fit our mish-mosh of obscure automobiles. Of the 16 questionable decisions (read: cars) I currently have to my name, only about half of them were meant to be sold in the U.S. And of those, none are what you’d call ordinary.


In order to make progress on just about any project, we have to get pretty creative. Work on the Simca 1000S Bertone has continued this week, but at a suboptimal pace. While trying to get the engine running, we struggled with slow cranking speed. When it became apparent that the starter was dead, chief deckhand Thomas dutifully extracted it from the rear of the car and got the unit onto the bench.


Yes, we have several Simca manuals in the Troutman Foundry library.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Things got weird from there. Thomas started scratching the dirt off of the starter’s Paris-Rhone body, solenoid, and armature in the hopes of finding a part number and cross-referencing to something much less obscure. Even a substitute part from some other Simca that’s slightly more common than the 1000S Brtone would have been nice.


Upon not-so-close inspection, it became clear that a master of the craft had been there before us.


D8E45


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Life on the prairie is hard. One must improvise.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Let the diag begin.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Adapted to the starter body—by way of a piece of muffler tubing, silicone, and pan head screws—was an AC Delco starter solenoid from a[small-block Chevrolet](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/chevy-small-block-the-little-engine-that-did/) . Obviously, some cattle rancher (from the prairie we rescued the Simca from in Nebraska) was in a desperate situation like ours and simply did whatever he could. As I was told once while trying to cross-reference radiator caps for a ’55 Cadillac, at a Carquest, in the middle of nowhere, North Dakota, “Life on the prairie is tough.” Inspirational.


Now the question remains: Should we rebuild this very starter with the Chevrolet solenoid as a rolling monument to our literal and figurative cowboy of automotive cross-referencing? Or should it just go up on the Healing Shelf?


Two potential options surfaced immediately: 1) Buying Hitachi-based starters with a custom nose housing—aimed at hill climb cars overseas, and thus, expensive. 2) Buying an entire Simca 1000 sedan, down in Georgia, that had rotted in half. The rust was so bad on the latter option that I could actually see in the online listing’s photos that the starter was still present and resting on the ground with the engine. Convenient!


I messaged the seller. Unfortunately, it was all or nothing; I couldn’t just buy the gas cap and starter. I’d have to take the entire crap pile for the last two good parts on the car… that is, if such a crust bucket would even load.


Has starter. Photo courtesy of the seller.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Factoring in gas, Thomas’s time, and the purchase price (even at scrap value), I’d be looking at $600 for a questionable starter and a good story. In a rare moment of restraint, I hit pause… for now.


If I *were* to repair the existing unit on the car, I’d need a solenoid and[field winding](https://www.dukeelectric.com/blog/types-of-motor-windings-and-how-to-test-for-failure/) . Considering all the holes drilled into the nose housing, I’d ideally need a core, too.


Meanwhile, I started diving alarmingly deep into these French starters from Paris Rhone. It turns out that I have what’s called a D8E series, or more specifically, a D8E4—a 9-spline, left-hand rotation unit used in a small-ish list of vehicles. If only I could find a Renault R3, R4, or R5! On the Simca Club America Facebook group, I got a non-committal (but potentially helpful) answer that a Fiat 850 starter *may* fit.


(Side note: You may be thinking, Matt, isn’t a LeCar an R5?! If only it were that easy: The LeCar was a U.S. market car and had the larger D9-series starter. *Merde* !)


According to further research into interchange guides (thank you, Hagerty commenters), the Renault R4 was fitted with the D8E45 as well as a D8E74… which cross-references to a (drum roll, please….) *Toro golf course mower sold with a Renault engine* ! Such a thing sells on eBay for the price of a solenoid from France. I ordered one.


Meanwhile, we have started down the path of procuring brake components for the Simca, and there is absolutely no shortage of new-old-stock, dare I say, *garbage* on eBay. Many years back, I bought about a half dozen new-old-stock Simca 1204 master cylinders, only to find that absolutely all of the rubber had turned back into organic matter. I unsatisfactorily rebuilt one with Ford Ranger parts, and the rear brakes never worked again. I think that’s enough Simca master cylinder PTSD for one lifetime, so I have opened my eyes to retrofitting something suitable.


After a bit more research, we have determined that the best course involves mounting racing master cylinders in place of the standard clutch and brake units. Specifically, the Tilton 74 series with a 7/8″ bore. In parallel, I did locate the seals for relatively cheap (but in France), so I may try that route before throwing up my hands and adapting the Tiltons.


Thomas was ultimately able to find most of the caliper rebuild components, so 60-year-old French disc brakes might not be as bad to rebuild as we expected. Of course, it’s unclear if the 1000S Bertone ever came with rear discs at all… but this example mysteriously has them. I think I’ll roll the dice and order the cheap seal kits before giving up.


I’m about 7/8″ away from putting Tiltons on this.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Moving on to the Simca’s wheel situation: I was able to find a little bit more information about the[Shelby Viper Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/against-all-oddities-vive-la-simca/) mag wheels, and they are not particularly valuable. Just another instance of loaning the Shelby name out in the 1970s. Neither Thomas nor I felt guilty about rattle-can-bombing these things in silver mist and popping them on the car temporarily. Of course, installing them requires a vintage mag *bolt* (does that even exist?). As you may imagine, my search for any Simca-specific help came up dry, but the vintage racing community has a plethora of knowledge on stud conversions and mag lugs to fit first-wave alloy wheels like this.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


So there you have it. Precious little progress, but a lot learned in the research phase. And I’ll find out shortly if a Toro Lawn Groundsmaster 327 starter fits a Bertone Simca.
